misconceptions.description: Believing removing names and SSNs is sufficient to anonymize a behavioral dataset
misconceptions.trigger: learner says 'we removed PII, the dataset is anonymous'
misconceptions.feedback: Quasi-identifiers (zip, DOB, gender, behavioral patterns) can link to auxiliary data and re-identify records. Sweeney's 87% result is the canonical demonstration.

misconceptions.description: Assuming trained models cannot leak training data after the data is locked away
misconceptions.trigger: learner releases a model trained on sensitive data without privacy auditing
misconceptions.feedback: Models leak via membership inference, attribute inference, and verbatim memorization. Releasing a model is closer to releasing a lossy view of the training data than to releasing nothing.

misconceptions.description: Believing differential privacy provides perfect anonymity with no utility cost
misconceptions.trigger: learner cites DP as a one-size-fits-all privacy fix
misconceptions.feedback: DP bounds per-individual leakage by a parameter ε. Smaller ε means stronger privacy and lower utility. Choosing ε is itself a policy decision, not a technical default.

misconceptions.description: Evaluating privacy harm one record at a time without considering aggregation
misconceptions.trigger: learner argues 'each data point is mundane, so the system is not invasive'
misconceptions.feedback: Joining mundane streams produces invasive profiles. Surveillance-by-aggregation is the threat that data minimization, purpose limitation, and retention limits are designed to bound.
